topics.title: 24.1 Page-table entries
topics.summary: A page-table entry encodes mapping information and control bits. Depending on its level and configuration, it can point to another table or describe a mapped page. It may include a physical address, presence information, access permissions, and status used by memory-management policy. An entry is not a portable C structure whose bit layout can be guessed from a diagram for another architecture. Kernel code must follow the architecture’s encoding and required update procedures. Ordinary user programs should reason about the behavior exposed by mapping APIs instead of attempting to manipulate active page tables.

topics.title: 24.2 Present bit
topics.summary: A present indicator tells hardware whether an entry is valid for the corresponding translation step. An absent entry can cause a page fault. The kernel may use nonpresent encodings and its own metadata to remember whether the region is demand-paged, swapped, invalid, or associated with another policy. Therefore, “not present” does not automatically mean “read this page from disk.” The handler must first establish that the access is legitimate. A zero-filled anonymous page may require no file read at all. A completely invalid address must not be repaired by granting access merely because a fault occurred.

topics.title: 24.3 Writable bit
topics.summary: A writable permission controls whether stores are allowed under the architecture’s access rules. A mapping can be readable without being writable. Copy-on-write commonly uses a temporarily nonwritable hardware mapping for a region that is logically permitted to become privately writable after a fault. Permission interpretation can involve multiple levels and processor controls. It is unsafe to inspect only one leaf bit and conclude that an access must succeed. The complete translation and protection state determines the result. This chapter’s exercises state a simplified combined-permission rule explicitly.

topics.title: 24.4 User-accessible bit
topics.summary: A user/supervisor permission distinguishes mappings accessible to user-mode code from mappings reserved for privileged access. It helps prevent an application from treating kernel data as ordinary user memory even when some related address range exists in the broader translation structure. This hardware distinction does not replace file permissions, process credentials, or application authorization. A user-accessible buffer may still contain data that an application should not disclose to a particular network client. Memory-access enforcement and application-level information policy operate at different layers.

topics.title: 24.5 Multilevel page tables
topics.summary: A multilevel design divides the virtual page number into several indexes. Each index selects an entry in the current table; that entry leads to the next level until a mapping is found. Large-page entries can terminate a walk earlier when the architecture supports them. A familiar x86-64 example uses four levels with 9 index bits per level and a 12-bit offset, describing a 48-bit virtual-address organization subject to canonical-address rules. Other configurations can add a fifth level and expand the address width. The exact layout is a platform fact, not a consequence of the C++ pointer type alone. [ R3 , R10 ]

topics.title: 24.7 Memory protection
topics.summary: Protection checks combine the requested operation with the applicable mapping permissions and architectural state. Reading data, writing data, and fetching instructions are not necessarily governed by identical permissions. Non-executable mappings help separate data storage from executable code. Changing a page-table entry is not enough when processors retain cached translations based on the old state. The system must perform the required invalidation and coordination. On a multicore system, other cores may also hold relevant translations; this is the reason for translation invalidation mechanisms often discussed as TLB shootdowns.

topics.title: Worked example — A two-level address decomposition
topics.summary: Use a 16-bit teaching address space with 256-byte pages and two levels of 16-entry tables. The address fields are: Address 0xABCD yields outer index 0xA , inner index 0xB , and offset 0xCD . Suppose outer entry A points to a valid inner table and inner entry B maps frame 0x34 . The translated address is 0x34CD in a physical model that supports that frame number. Now add permissions. The outer entry allows user reads and writes, but the inner entry allows only user reads. A user load succeeds; a user store fails. For this model, effective permissions are the intersection of the permissions along the path. Giving the outer entry more authority cannot override a restrictive leaf entry. A flat table for all 256 virtual pages needs 256 entries. The two-level arrangement needs one 16-entry outer table plus 16 entries for each allocated inner table. With only one populated inner table, it uses 32 entries; with all 16 inner tables allocated, it uses 272 entries. Hierarchy saves space for sparse mappings but is not automatically smaller for a fully populated tiny address space.
